en: Once it had grown wrathful, Bakai,
It would not go idly without drinking blood, Bakai.
Without watering Zulpukor with blood, Bakai,
I will not turn back downcast, Bakai!”
When the leopard stood there raging,
Refusing to heed anyone,
From the raid on India and the taking of spoils,
From the attack upon that people,
When the realm with its palace was destroyed,
There were eleven elephants taken as booty.
The khan's doorway was Judgment Day, my son.
Almambet and Chubak, the paired heroes, my son,
Said, “Let this serve for your rite,” my son,
Leading two elephants, my son!
“Here is the sovereign city and land, my friend;
If you would take a head, here we stand, my friend!
Here are the Kyrgyz people with their cities, my friend;
If you would shed blood, here we stand, my friend!
Give the vast herds of the Chinese, my friend.
If you truly are a khan, my friend,
We ask it of you with all our hearts, my friend:
Grant the life of our sister-in-law Kanykei, my friend!
Find a way, somehow find it, my friend.
If you must perform your rite, my friend,
Strike off the heads of these two elephants, my friend!”
Blood-drinking Manas, that dear lion,
Your heroic father in his wrath,
Seized the blood-drinking sword Zulpukor
At its sheath,
Drew it out by the hilt,
His fury taking life.
When he swung Zulpukor,
Life left the kneeling elephant.
Unless it had drunk its fill of blood,
Your khan father's Zulpukor
Would not fit back into its sheath.
When drawn in surging might,
It would not lie idle without drinking blood.
Yesterday, the two khans, Azhybai and Bakai,
When they offered their weighty words,
For me, your wretched mother,
The two khans somehow managed
To plead for my life.
He had heroism but no sense,
Was a somewhat simple-minded soul;
Your father cared nothing for dying.
A lion like your father
Almighty Allah
Will never create again.
There is no person like him.
I, your mother Kanykei,
Have seen that happen many times.
I have no strength to tell it.
For having spoken openly,
Your mother was left without a spoonful of blood.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
My noble son, listen:
Such is this shitty world!
If I turned and spoke again,
Your leopard father Manas
Stood ready to dig my grave,
To boil my bitter misery,
To show before my eyes
Strange suffering no mortal had seen.
Your father Manas rose as khan.
Whenever he grew wrathful,
His might took lives.
The Chinese who came from Beijing,
If they settled beside him—
I feared what they would do to your father.
I thought God would openly
Strike your father down.
Those Chinese who had wandered here,
Deceiving the guileless man,
Would together bring about his end, I thought,
“Your doomed father Manas—
They will cut off his head and go”—
For saying this I took a beating.
When your father abused me,
Against my flesh, calico dresses—
I wore ten, one over another.
That the unbeliever was different,
I, your mother, knew from the first day.
When he settled in the neighboring camp,
When he learned the inner secrets,
Against your father a rebellion—
I thought he would raise one.
If your father fell into his hands,
He would make him tremble like a lean sheep,
I thought he would seize him.
Tying up your father's head,
To the khagan, khan of khans,
That accursed man, claiming a reward for the news,
Would go, I thought.
The great khanship of Beijing—
I thought he would take it.
Great turmoil upon your father—
I thought he would bring it.
My reckoning turned badly against me.
For wanting to speak openly,
By your guileless father Manas
I had my side whipped open.
When Közkaman was coming to settle,
Your father beat me terribly.
Only a spoonful of my blood remained;
My flesh was left bruised and wasted.
Yet death did not come.
I survived without dying.
When your heroic father lashed me repeatedly,
Only after three months was I barely fit again.
I suffered much torment.
Like some foolish wife,
At your lion father himself,
I, this wretched soul, did not knit my brows
Or speak in protest.
These are the robes I have taken off.
My noble son, listen.
I have many strange things to tell.
Why should I tell the rest?
My foal, let me tell what comes next.
My lament is a white palace.
I will tell much of my sorrow.
Without grieving, orphan, listen!
Your father Manas Khan
Tied my days in a tight knot.
Though I pleaded, he would not heed my words.
He dug my broad grave,
Showed before my eyes
Suffering no person had seen.
Kökchököz and Közkaman,
Enemies who openly came,
Deceived your father, those fools,
Sending six swift horses,
Sending a palm-sized letter.
When he saw that letter,
Ormombek of the Odugan,
Zhamgyrchy of the Eshtek,
And Shygai Khan of Alkym—
He sent those three,
Had swift horses readied for transport,
Fat young lambs and savory heads
Properly boiled,
Sugar heaped like snow,
Butter piled in great mounds.
He went out to greet them as kin,
The enemies who would cast him into hell.
Your mountain-like father knew nothing.
Your guileless father, the gray-maned lion,
Calling the Chinese his kin,
Went there to meet them.
Sweet of speech, honey-tongued,
These were the enemies who came.
To your saintly father Manas,
They spoke half in jest, half in earnest:
“Unwearied by six months of riding,
Is generous Manas well?
We have come wandering from the Chinese.
Lion Manas, welcome us!
Was what I did so wrong?
We rode mules, calling them coursers;
We left the khagan, calling upon kin.
With much sorrow in our hearts,
We rubbed this Kongkulboz's back sore.
When we left the Chinese,
Saying there were lands called Zhylyngduu and Köng-Kol,
We came fleeing and wandering,
Saying there was a leopard who would value us,
A lion such as Manas.
We went to the khagan and settled there.
Leopard Manas, listen:
The many Chinese who followed the khagan
Drove us about under guard.
Unable to endure their oppression,
We fled and wandered, seeking a place to live,
Placing our hope in Zhakyp's only son.
The great Manchu host, the many Chinese—
Manas, my shelter, listen:
Those Chinese seized
My yearling to slaughter in the steppe.
If you truly are a lion,
Find for me, leopard Manas,
A place where I may go!
We were the ones who broke away and fled;
Be the one who finds a remedy!
Walking has worn us out; give us a yearling.
Manas, we are thirsty; give us tea!
We have been severed; join us together.
If you truly are a khan,
Manas, we are scattered; gather us!
We are thin; fatten these bodies.
We are hungry; fill our bellies.
We are cold; give us robes.
King Manas, my kinsman,
We have been brought to such want;
Give us wealth in plenty!
Kongurbai at the khagan's court—
We suffered oppression from the Manchu.
From the Kara-Kytai and many Shibe
We suffered violence.
We paid many levies and taxes
And come here without strength.
I have no yearling to straddle;
We come here unable to acquire livestock.
Toward the khagan's sorrow-laden land,
We fled on foot by day and night,
To the one who would ease our sorrow,
My stalwart lion Manas.
We were bondslaves under the khagan.
Welcome this stalwart soul.
O Sultan Manas, heed my words.
Leopard Manas, lion,
It is your custom to shelter a people.
These are the ones who came from the Kalmyks.
If you clash with an enemy,
They will be the wings that follow behind you.”
Kökchököz and Közkaman
Firmly spoke their words in turn,
As though friends had settled in the camp.
“Leopard Manas,” they said.
When he heard their many words,
Your guileless father rejoiced.
Those who came from the Kalmyks
He brought to settle in Talas.
Calling them his kin, he settled them;
The fugitives from the Kalmyks
He allowed to do as they wished.
When I considered it myself,
There was malice in their words.
If the accursed men had the strength,
They meant to strike me down.
There was something alien in their words,
Something different in their eyes.
Those accursed men who came apart from their people—
Now, my child, listen—
They meant to separate me away.
Like openly honest men,
They rode in and settled in Talas.
He became the closest kinsman
To your guileless father Manas.
The Chinese man who came horseless
Was given an argali-legged, bronze-limbed
Winged steed to ride.
The Chinese man who came without a robe
Was given one with golden collar, bronze sleeves,
Double mail, lark-eyed rings—
He clothed him in a coat no bullet could pierce.
The accursed man who came without a wife—
“Here is a kinswoman,” he said,
Scarlet dress, slender waist,
A beauty from among the Kyrgyz,
Your khan father gave him as a bride.
The accursed man who came without livestock
Received fine horses from the hills,
Thoroughbreds and coursers mingled;
He gave him swift steeds of every kind.
That feckless wretch
